back: Purpose to bring about the consequence, or knowledge to a substantial certainty that it will result (R2d § 8A; Garratt v. Dailey). Motive is irrelevant; children can intend.

front: Which torts does transferred intent cover?
back: Assault, battery, false imprisonment, trespass to land and trespass to chattels: intent transfers between victims and among these five torts. Not IIED or conversion.

Act intended to cause a harmful or offensive contact (or imminent apprehension of one) that results in a harmful or offensive contact with Π's person, including things closely connected to it. Offensive = offends a reasonable sense of dignity.

front: Does battery require Π's awareness or actual injury?
back: No. A sleeping Π can be battered, and nominal damages are available for an offensive touch without harm.

Act intended to cause harmful or offensive contact or apprehension, causing Π's reasonable apprehension of an imminent harmful or offensive contact. Π must be aware; future threats and (usually) words alone are not enough; apparent ability suffices.

Intent to confine; confinement within boundaries fixed by Δ (barriers, force, threats, asserted legal authority, duress); no reasonable known means of escape; Π aware of the confinement or harmed by it.
Extreme and outrageous conduct; intent or recklessness; causation; severe emotional distress (R2d § 46). Outrageous = beyond all bounds of decency.

front: IIED: when can a third person recover (R2d § 46(2))?
back: When Δ's outrageous conduct is directed at another: (a) immediate family member present, if Δ knows of presence; (b) any other person present, if bodily harm results. California: conduct directed at Π or in presence of Π known to Δ (Christensen).

front: Trespass to land: rule and the mistake point
back: Intentional entry onto land in Π's possession (or causing a thing or person to enter, or remaining after permission ends). Intent to enter suffices; a mistaken belief of right is no defense; no harm needed.

front: California: is noise or odor a trespass?
back: Not unless it causes physical damage to the property; otherwise it is a nuisance (Wilson v. Interlake Steel (1982) 32 Cal.3d 229).
Trespass to chattels: intentional dispossession, or intermeddling causing actual harm; damages = loss. Conversion: serious interference justifying a forced sale; damages = full value at conversion.
Extent and duration of control; intent to assert a right; good faith; harm done; inconvenience and expense to Π.

front: Is a good-faith purchaser from a thief liable for conversion?
back: Yes. Good faith is no defense; a thief passes no title. (A buyer from one with voidable title, or from an entrusted merchant, may take good title, UCC § 2-403.)

Express; apparent (conduct reasonably read as consent); customary; implied by law in emergencies. Requires capacity; limited to scope; vitiated by fraud as to the essential nature of the act or by duress.

front: Consent to an illegal act (mutual combat): effective?
back: Courts divide. Traditional rule: ineffective, so each combatant may sue. Restatement (R2d § 892C): effective. Either way, ineffective where a statute protects a class against its own consent.
Reasonable force against force reasonably believed imminent; deadly force only against a reasonably perceived threat of death or serious bodily harm; reasonable mistake protected; no retaliation.

front: Defense of others: majority vs. minority
back: Majority: privileged if the actor reasonably believes the third person may defend himself (mistake protected). Minority: actor steps into the shoes of the person defended.

front: Defense of property: can deadly force or a spring gun be used?
back: No. Only reasonable nondeadly force after a request to desist; a device is privileged only to the extent the owner could use the force in person (Katko v. Briney).
Detention on reasonable belief of theft, in a reasonable manner, for a reasonable time, on or near the premises. Reasonable mistake protected.
Wrongful taking; fresh pursuit; demand first unless futile; reasonable nondeadly force. Mistake not protected.

front: Private citizen's arrest for a felony
back: Privileged only if the felony was in fact committed and the citizen reasonably believed the arrestee committed it.
Public: complete privilege to avert public disaster, no liability. Private: incomplete privilege; entrant cannot be expelled but must pay actual damage (Vincent v. Lake Erie).
Duty; breach; actual cause; proximate cause; damages (actual harm).
Cardozo (majority): duty only to plaintiffs in the zone of foreseeable danger. Andrews: duty to all injured if a duty is owed to anyone; limits come through proximate cause.

front: California general duty and Rowland factors
back: Civ. Code § 1714(a) general duty of ordinary care. Exceptions only where public policy clearly supports them, weighing foreseeability, certainty of injury, closeness of connection, moral blame, preventing future harm, burden and consequences, insurance (Rowland; applied categorically, Cabral).
Employers owe no duty to employees' household members to prevent take-home COVID-19 (Rowland policy factors); the derivative-injury doctrine did not bar the spouse's claim.
Special relationship (carrier, innkeeper, business, custodian, school, employer); Δ created the peril; voluntary undertaking (liable if it increases risk or induces reliance); statute or contract.

front: California two-step for duty to protect from third parties
back: Brown v. USA Taekwondo: (1) is there a special relationship or other basis creating a duty? (2) If so, do the Rowland factors limit it?

Therapist liable only if the patient communicated a serious threat of physical violence against a reasonably identifiable victim; duty discharged by reasonable efforts to warn the victim and a law-enforcement agency.

Danger invites rescue: negligent Δ owes a duty to rescuers. Firefighter's rule: public safety professionals cannot recover for inherent risks of responding to the negligence that summoned them (CA: not private safety employees, Neighbarger; § 1714.9 exceptions).

front: Reasonable person: physical vs. mental conditions
back: Physical disability: reasonable person with that disability. Mental illness or low intelligence: no allowance. Superior skill must be used. Sudden unforeseeable incapacity is not negligence.
Reasonable child of like age, intelligence and experience, except adult activities (driving, boating), where the adult standard applies.
Knowledge and skill of a member of the profession in good standing (specialists: specialty standard; national standard trend); usually proven by expert testimony.

CA (Cobbs) and many states: disclose material risks a reasonable patient would consider significant; many others use a reasonable-physician standard (MBE: apply the stem's standard). Causation is objective: would a reasonable patient have refused? California also requires disclosure of the risks of refusing a test (Truman).

front: Common carriers: standard of care in California
back: Utmost care and diligence for carriers of persons for reward (Civ. Code § 2100); traditionally the highest degree of care consistent with practical operation.
Negligent if B < P × L: burden of precautions less than probability of harm times gravity of the loss (Carroll Towing).

front: Is compliance with industry custom conclusive?
back: No. Custom is evidence of due care, not conclusive (The T.J. Hooper). For professionals, the profession's custom sets the standard.

front: Negligence per se: elements and effect
back: Statute defines conduct; Π within the protected class; harm of the type targeted; unexcused violation → negligence per se (duty and breach). Causation and damages still required.

front: California: effect of a statutory violation (Evid. Code § 669)
back: Presumption of negligence if the violation proximately caused injury of the kind the statute aimed at, to a member of the protected class; rebuttable by showing reasonable conduct of one who desired to comply.
Incapacity; no knowledge of the occasion; inability after diligence; emergency not of Δ's making; compliance would be more dangerous (Tedla v. Ellman).

front: Res ipsa loquitur: elements and effect
back: Accident ordinarily does not happen without negligence; Δ's exclusive control (other causes eliminated); → permissible inference of negligence, enough to reach the jury. California: presumption affecting the burden of producing evidence (Evid. Code § 646).
An unconscious surgical patient may use res ipsa against all defendants who had control of his body, each of whom must explain.

front: Slip-and-fall: what must Π show if Δ did not create the hazard?
back: Actual or constructive notice: the hazard existed long enough that reasonable inspection would have discovered and fixed it.
Δ's negligence is an actual cause if the harm would not have happened without it. Focus on the negligent aspect of the conduct.
When two causes each alone would have produced the harm (merged fires), each is an actual cause if a substantial factor. California uses substantial factor generally (Mitchell v. Gonzales).
Two negligent hunters, one unidentified shot: burden shifts to each Δ to prove he did not cause the harm.
Fungible product, unidentifiable maker, substantial share of market joined: each Δ liable for its market share (Sindell); several only (Brown v. Superior Court).

front: Joint and several liability: rule and MBE default
back: Each Δ whose conduct caused an indivisible injury is liable for the whole; Π may collect from any (once). MBE default: joint and several with pure comparative negligence.
California: economic damages joint and several; non-economic damages several only, in proportion to each Δ's fault. No reduction for an intentional tortfeasor (B.B., 2020).

Partial equitable indemnity by comparative fault (American Motorcycle); good-faith settlement reduces others' liability by the amount paid and bars contribution claims against the settlor (CCP §§ 877, 877.6; Tech-Bilt).
Harm within the scope of the risk that made the conduct negligent: foreseeable type of harm to a foreseeable plaintiff. Manner and extent need not be foreseeable (Wagon Mound No. 1; R3d PEH § 29).
Δ takes Π as he finds him and is liable for the full extent of harm, even if a pre-existing condition made it unusually severe.

front: Which intervening causes are NOT superseding?
back: Foreseeable ones: medical malpractice in treating the injury, rescuers, foreseeable negligence of others, reactions/escape, later disease, crimes Δ's negligence made foreseeable.

front: When is an intervening act superseding?
back: When it is unforeseeable and extraordinary, e.g., an independent intentional crime that Δ's conduct did not make more likely, or an unforeseeable act of God producing a different kind of harm.

Undiscovered: refrain from willful/wanton harm. Discovered or anticipated: reasonable care in active operations; warn of known, concealed, artificial conditions involving risk of death or serious harm.

Possessor knows children likely to trespass; artificial condition with unreasonable risk of death/serious harm to children; children don't appreciate risk due to youth; burden of eliminating slight vs. risk; failure of reasonable care.
Warn of or make safe known concealed dangers; reasonable care in active operations; no duty to inspect. Social guests are licensees.
Reasonable care including inspection to discover dangers, then warn or repair; reasonable care in operations; status ends outside the scope of the invitation.

Rowland v. Christian abolished entrant categories: reasonable care to all under § 1714; status is a factor. Civ. Code § 846 recreational-use immunity (exceptions: willful/malicious, consideration, express invitation).

front: Lessor's exceptions to no duty after transfer
back: Known latent dangers not disclosed; common areas retained; promise to repair or negligent repair; lease for public admission; short-term furnished dwelling. CA: § 1714 reasonable care; no strict liability (Peterson).

front: Ann M. and Delgado: security against crime
back: Hiring guards requires heightened foreseeability (usually prior similar incidents); a sliding scale applies: minimal precautions may be required on lesser foreseeability.
Π within the zone of physical danger who fears for own safety may recover; many courts require physical manifestation of the distress.

front: Thing v. La Chusa: bystander requirements
back: Π (1) closely related to the injury victim; (2) present at the scene of the injury-producing event when it occurs and then aware it is causing injury; (3) suffers serious emotional distress beyond that of a disinterested witness.

front: Can an unmarried cohabitant recover as a bystander in California?
back: No under Elden v. Sheldon (1988), but the California Supreme Court granted review in Sanchez v. Rojas to reconsider; check status before the exam.
NIED is negligence; a direct victim recovers serious emotional distress where Δ's duty was assumed, imposed by law, or arose from a relationship (e.g., obstetrician to mother; Molien misdiagnosis).

front: Potter v. Firestone: fear of cancer
back: Recoverable only if Π's fear stems from corroborated knowledge that cancer is more likely than not to develop from the exposure (relaxed for oppression, fraud or malice).
Spouses and registered domestic partners recover; children cannot for loss of a parent (Borer); unmarried cohabitants cannot (Elden, under review). Derivative claim.

front: Wrongful death: who sues and what is recovered (California)
back: CCP § 377.60 heirs (spouse, domestic partner, children; dependents). Damages: lost support and services, funeral costs, loss of love, companionship, comfort, care, society. Not grief, not decedent's pain, not punitive damages.
Decedent's pre-death losses (medical, lost earnings to death) and punitive damages; no pain, suffering or disfigurement for actions filed on or after Jan 1, 2026 (the SB 447 window closed).

front: MBE assumption on survival and wrongful death
back: Assume both actions are available unless the question says otherwise.
Generally no duty to strangers; recovery only with a special relationship (J'Aire / Biakanja factors). No duty to businesses closed by a gas leak (Southern California Gas Leak Cases).
Conduct of the kind employed to perform, substantially within authorized time and space, motivated at least partly to serve the employer. Detour in; frolic out; commuting out (with exceptions).

front: When is an employee's intentional tort within scope?
back: When force is part of the job (bouncer), it arises from a work dispute, or it is meant to serve the employer. California: engendered by or a foreseeable outgrowth of the employment (Lisa M.; Mary M.).
Hirer's own negligence (selection, instruction, supervision); inherently dangerous or peculiar-risk work; nondelegable duties (public premises, statutory duties, carriers); apparent agency.
Hirer generally not liable to an independent contractor's own employees, unless retained control affirmatively contributed (Hooker) or a known concealed hazard was not disclosed (Kinsman).

front: Vehicle owners and bailors: vicarious liability?
back: None at common law (except family-purpose doctrine); liable for own negligent entrustment. California: owner liable for permissive user up to statutory limits (Veh. Code §§ 17150–17151).

front: Are parents vicariously liable for children's torts?
back: Not at common law; liable for own negligence in failing to control a child with known dangerous tendencies; statutes (CA Civ. Code § 1714.1) impose capped liability for willful misconduct.

Furnishing alcohol is not the proximate cause of resulting injuries (Civ. Code § 1714(b)–(c); B&P § 25602), except a licensee selling to an obviously intoxicated minor (§ 25602.1) or an adult host knowingly furnishing to someone under 21 at home (§ 1714(d)).
In a contributory-negligence jurisdiction, a negligent Π still recovers if Δ had the last clear opportunity to avoid the harm and failed to use it. Abolished in comparative-fault jurisdictions.
Pure: Π's recovery reduced by Π's %, even above 50% (California, Li; MBE default). Modified: barred at 50% (equal) or 51% (greater) fault.

front: Compute: Π damages $100,000; Π 60%, Δ 40% at fault. MBE default?
back: Pure comparative fault: Π recovers $40,000. (In a modified state, nothing.)

front: Express assumption of risk: when unenforceable?
back: Unclear language; gross negligence, recklessness or intentional harm (City of Santa Barbara); public-interest transactions (Tunkl factors); in California, exemption from fraud, willful injury or violation of law (Civ. Code § 1668).
Π knew and appreciated a specific risk and voluntarily encountered it; complete bar at common law; merged into comparative fault in most comparative states (secondary).

front: Knight v. Jewett: primary vs. secondary assumption of risk
back: Primary: no duty to protect against risks inherent in the activity (complete bar). Secondary: Δ owes a duty but Π knowingly encounters the risk → comparative fault.

front: Co-participant and coach liability in California sports
back: Co-participants liable only for intentional injury or conduct totally outside the range of ordinary activity in the sport; coaches liable for intentional injury or reckless conduct outside ordinary coaching (Kahn).

front: Duty of facility operators for inherent risks (California)
back: No duty to eliminate inherent risks, but a duty not to increase them beyond those inherent (Avila: hit by pitch is inherent).

front: Intrafamily and charitable immunity in California
back: Interspousal abolished (Self; Klein); parent–child abolished with reasonable-parent standard (Gibson); charitable abolished (Malloy v. Fong).
Discretionary-function exception (§ 2680(a)); most intentional torts (§ 2680(h)), except listed torts by law-enforcement officers.

No common-law liability (Gov. Code § 815); vicarious for employees within scope (§ 815.2); employee discretionary immunity for policy decisions (§ 820.2); dangerous condition of public property (§ 835); no punitive damages (§ 818).

front: Gov. Code § 835: dangerous condition of public property
back: Dangerous condition at time of injury; proximate cause; reasonably foreseeable risk of the kind of injury; employee's negligent act created it, or entity had actual or constructive notice in time to fix it.

front: California limitations periods: personal injury, defamation, fraud
back: Personal injury and wrongful death: 2 years (CCP § 335.1). Libel, slander, false imprisonment: 1 year (§ 340(c)). Fraud: 3 years from discovery (§ 338(d)).
High risk; likely great harm; risk not eliminable by reasonable care; not common usage; inappropriate to place; value outweighed by danger.

front: Scope limit on strict liability for abnormally dangerous activities
back: Liability only for harm of the kind that makes the activity abnormally dangerous, to foreseeable plaintiffs (e.g., mink frightened by blasting noise often outside the risk).
Wild animals: strict liability for characteristic dangers, even if tame. Domestic animals: only with known abnormal dangerous propensity. Trespassing livestock: strict liability.
Owner strictly liable when the dog bites a person in a public place or lawfully in a private place, regardless of prior viciousness or the owner's knowledge; bites only.

Comparative fault (MBE default; CA): Π's negligence, even a knowing unreasonable encounter, reduces recovery. Contributory-negligence states: failure to discover is no defense; knowing unreasonable encounter (assumption of risk) is a complete bar. Express AOR can bar; abnormally sensitive activity of Π.

front: Strict products liability: prima facie case
back: Commercial seller; product defective when it left Δ; reached Π without substantial change; actual and proximate cause; physical injury or other property damage (Greenman; R2d § 402A).

front: California strict products liability: is 'unreasonably dangerous' required?
back: No (Cronin v. J.B.E. Olson Corp.).
Product departs from its intended design (differs from other units), even if all possible care was used; may be inferred from circumstances (malfunction doctrine).

Consumer expectations: failed to perform as safely as an ordinary consumer would expect in intended or reasonably foreseeable use. Risk-utility: risks outweigh benefits, usually shown by a feasible safer alternative design.
California: under risk-benefit, once Π shows the design proximately caused injury, Δ must prove the design's benefits outweigh its risks.
Consumer-expectations test applies only where everyday experience lets ordinary consumers form minimum safety expectations; complex technical failures use risk-benefit.
Gravity of the danger; likelihood; feasibility of a safer alternative design; cost of improved design; adverse consequences to product and consumer of the alternative.

Foreseeable risks known or reasonably knowable at distribution that reasonable warnings would have reduced; no duty to warn of obvious risks; California requires knowability even in strict liability (Anderson).

Maker of prescription drugs or devices warns the physician, not the patient. California (Himes, 2024): Π need not show the doctor would not have prescribed; causation if the doctor would have passed a stronger warning on and a prudent patient would have declined.

front: Who is strictly liable for defective products?
back: All commercial sellers in the chain: manufacturers, component makers, distributors, retailers (Vandermark), commercial lessors (Price v. Shell). Not casual sellers, service providers (Murphy), or landlords (Peterson).
Express/implied assumption, de facto merger, mere continuation, fraud; California adds product-line continuation (Ray v. Alad).

front: Who may recover in strict products liability, and for what?
back: Users, consumers and foreseeable bystanders (Elmore); personal injury and damage to other property; not purely economic loss or damage to the product itself (Seely).
Only unforeseeable misuse defeats liability; foreseeable misuse must be designed or warned against. Substantial unforeseeable alteration is a defense.

front: Comparative fault in strict products liability
back: Reduces Π's recovery (Daly v. General Motors); mere failure to discover a defect is not a defense in contributory states.

front: Subsequent remedial measures in California product cases
back: Admissible to prove defect in strict products liability (Ault; Evid. Code § 1151), unlike FRE 407.
Duty of reasonable care in design, manufacture, inspection and warning to all foreseeable users (MacPherson, no privity); requires proof of fault; retailers usually no duty to inspect.

Express (§ 2-313: affirmation, description, sample; basis of the bargain); merchantability (§ 2-314: merchant; ordinary purpose); fitness (§ 2-315: particular purpose + reliance). Disclaimer, notice (§ 2-607) and privity issues.
Commercial seller's public misrepresentation of a material fact about a product: strict liability for physical harm from justifiable reliance, even without fraud or negligence.

Substantial and unreasonable interference with another's use and enjoyment of land; substantial = offensive to a normal person; unreasonable = gravity of harm outweighs utility (or serious harm Δ could compensate).
Public officials; a private person only with special injury different in kind from the public's (CA Civ. Code § 3493).
A factor in reasonableness, not a complete bar (R2d § 840D).
Damages (permanent vs. continuing); injunction if damages inadequate and hardships balance; permanent damages in lieu (Boomer); reasonable self-help abatement after notice.
Defamatory statement of fact; of and concerning Π; publication to a third person; damages (presumed or special); plus falsity and fault where the Constitution requires.
Serious crime; loathsome disease; business, trade or profession; serious sexual misconduct. California § 46 also lists impotence/want of chastity and words causing actual damage.
Libel defamatory on its face needs no proof of special damages; libel requiring extrinsic facts (per quod) requires special damages.
Π proves falsity and actual malice (knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard: serious doubts) by clear and convincing evidence (NYT v. Sullivan; Curtis Publishing; St. Amant).
Π proves falsity and at least negligence; presumed or punitive damages require actual malice; otherwise actual injury only. California requires negligence (Brown v. Kelly Broadcasting).
Presumed and punitive damages available without actual malice; common-law rules apply.
Only if it does not assert or imply a provably false fact (Milkovich); rhetorical hyperbole protected; no separate opinion privilege.

front: Qualified privilege: how is it lost?
back: Abuse: knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard (or, in some states, ill will as primary purpose), excessive publication, improper purpose.

(a) official duty; (b) legislative, judicial, official proceedings (absolute litigation privilege; bars all torts except malicious prosecution, Silberg); (c) common interest without malice; (d) fair report of proceedings; (e) fair report of public meetings.
Appropriation of name or likeness; intrusion upon seclusion; public disclosure of private facts; false light (R2d §§ 652A–652E).

front: Public disclosure of private facts: elements; is truth a defense?
back: Publicity; private facts; highly offensive to a reasonable person; not of legitimate public concern. Truth is no defense.
Publicity placing Π in a false light highly offensive to a reasonable person; Δ's knowledge or reckless disregard (actual malice for matters of public interest, Time v. Hill).

Institution or continuation of proceedings; termination in Π's favor; no probable cause; malice; damages. California: probable cause is objective (Sheldon Appel); continuing without probable cause actionable (Zamos).
Ulterior purpose; willful act in the use of process not proper in the regular conduct of the proceeding; damages.
Misrepresentation of material fact; scienter (knowledge or recklessness); intent to induce reliance; actual and justifiable reliance; pecuniary damages.

front: When does silence become actionable fraud?
back: Duty to disclose: fiduciary relationship; half-truth; statement later learned to be false; material facts Π cannot reasonably discover (e.g., latent defects in a home). Active concealment always counts.

A contracting party may sue for fraudulent concealment during performance if the tort's elements exist independently of the contract and the conduct exposes Π to a risk of harm beyond the parties' reasonable contemplation; the economic loss rule does not bar it.

False information supplied in business or professional capacity for others' guidance, without reasonable care; liability to the limited class Δ intends to guide; justifiable reliance; pecuniary loss; comparative fault is a defense.

front: Bily v. Arthur Young: auditor liability
back: Negligence: client only. Negligent misrepresentation: specifically intended third-party beneficiaries. Fraud: any third party who relied.
Valid contract; Δ's knowledge; intentional acts designed to induce breach or disruption; actual breach or disruption; damages; improper interference (§ 767 factors).

front: California: interference with an at-will contract
back: Requires an independently wrongful act (Ixchel Pharma v. Biogen, extending Reeves v. Hanlon).

front: Interference with prospective economic advantage in California
back: Economic relationship with probable benefit; knowledge; intentional acts designed to disrupt; independently wrongful act (Della Penna; Korea Supply); actual disruption; damages.
False statement disparaging Π's products, business or title; publication; knowledge or reckless disregard; special damages (specific pecuniary loss).
Independent payments (insurance) do not reduce damages (Helfend), but past medical damages are limited to amounts actually paid or incurred (Howell).
In motor-vehicle cases, uninsured owners or operators and drivers convicted of DUI in connection with the accident cannot recover non-economic damages.

Clear and convincing evidence of oppression, fraud or malice; against an employer only via an officer, director or managing agent: advance knowledge of the employee's unfitness plus conscious disregard, authorization, ratification or own misconduct.

front: Where are punitive damages unavailable in California tort cases?
back: Wrongful-death actions (narrow felony-homicide exception); against public entities (Gov. Code § 818); breach of contract alone; no actual damages (a no-harm nominal award likely fails). Available in survival actions.
On the AB 35 schedule: $510,000 for non-death injury and $700,000 for wrongful death (from $350,000 / $500,000 in 2023, rising $40,000 / $50,000 a year). Verify the applicable date rule.
A maker of a nondefective drug owes no negligence duty in deciding whether and when to develop or commercialize a safer alternative (Rowland exception); reaffirms the defect-centered framework.
Build a Π × Δ grid from the call; for each pair: each tort's elements, defenses, damages; conclusion on every issue; general law first, then a one-line California rule where different.

front: MBE weight of negligence in Torts
back: About half of the 25 scored Torts questions; the other half come from intentional torts, strict/products liability and other torts together.
